title: Netiquette Guidelines
summary: Provides a minimal set of guidelines for network etiquette that organizations may adapt for their own use. It covers manners for one-to-one communication such as mail and talk, and for one-to-many communication such as lists and news. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet was growing faster than its own culture could be passed on, so this memo lists the expected manners for people online. It covers writing to one person, posting to a group, and using services that belong to someone else. Any organization can copy the list and change it to suit itself.

questions: how should i write email politely
subtitle: A short rulebook of good manners for email, talk, mailing lists, NetNews and information services.

tldr.problem: People who had grown up with the Internet knew its culture, but newcomers did not, and there was no single short list of the expected behaviours.
tldr.mechanism: The memo gives a minimum set of guidelines in a bulleted form, split into one-to-one communication, one-to-many communication and information services, with separate advice for users, administrators and moderators.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo, published as FYI 28, and not a standard. Organizations are free to take the list and adapt it for their own use.

facts.label: Talk line length
facts.value: No more than 70 characters and 12 lines

today: RFC 1855 is an Informational memo published as FYI 28 in October 1995, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes services of its time, such as Gopher, Wais and NetNews, and it is guidance for people rather than a specification that software implements.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1855 gives a minimum set of guidelines for network etiquette, which organizations may take and adapt for their own use. It is deliberately written in a bulleted format so that adaptation is easy and so that any one item is easy to find, and it serves as a minimum set of guidelines for individuals, both users and administrators. The memo is the product of the Responsible Use of the Network (RUN) Working Group of the IETF, and is published as FYI 28.

The reason it exists is stated in the first section. Earlier users of the Internet had grown up with it, were technically minded, and understood the transport and the protocols. The community now includes people who are new to the environment and who do not need to know about transport and protocols, so the guide offers a minimum set of behaviours to bring them into the Internet culture quickly.

The material is organized into three parts: one-to-one communication, covering mail and talk; one-to-many communication, covering mailing lists and NetNews; and information services, covering ftp, WWW, Wais, Gopher, MUDs and MOOs. A selected bibliography follows. Individual users are told to check with whoever supplies their access, since providers, universities and employers all have their own rules about ownership of mail and files, about what is proper to post or send, and about how to present yourself.
sections.plainLanguage: New people were joining an Internet built by people who already knew how it worked. This memo is a short list of the manners that helped newcomers fit in, and organizations were invited to copy and adapt it.

sections.title: One-to-One Communication: Mail and Talk
sections.content:
One-to-one communication is defined as talking with another person as if face to face, a dialog. Common courtesy matters more online, because body language and tone of voice have to be inferred. The mail advice is concrete. Unless you are using encryption, assume mail is not secure and never put in a message anything you would not put on a postcard. Respect copyright. If you forward or re-post a message, do not change its wording, and ask permission first if it was personal to you. Never send chain letters; the memo says chain letters are forbidden on the Internet and that your network privileges will be revoked.

There are also habits that make messages easier to read and cheaper to receive. Give the message a subject that reflects its content, and include a short signature, with a rule of thumb of no more than 4 lines. Use mixed case, because upper case looks as if you are shouting. Limit lines to fewer than 65 characters. Know how large a message you are sending, with a good rule of thumb of not sending a file larger than 50 Kilobytes, and consider file transfer or smaller pieces instead. Reply briefly and immediately when a message's importance justifies it, but wait overnight before sending an emotional response, and use FLAME ON and FLAME OFF enclosures to mark a strong opinion without the heat of an argument.

Two economic points are made. The cost of delivering a message is paid about equally by the sender and the recipient, unlike physical mail, telephone, television or radio, and sending mail also costs network bandwidth, disk space and processor time. The memo calls this a fundamental economic reason why unsolicited advertising by email is unwelcome. It also notes that mail and news are subject to forgery and spoofing of varying degrees of detectability, so a reality check is needed before treating a message as valid.

Talk, an interactive two-person session, has its own rules: write out no more than 70 characters and no more than 12 lines, use two carriage returns to signal that you are done, say goodbye and wait for a farewell before ending the session, remember that talk interrupts the other person, and never talk to strangers. Administrators are told to have written guidelines for illegal, improper or forged traffic, to handle requests by the next business day, to respond promptly to concerns about improper messages, to handle chain letter requests immediately, to explain system rules such as disk quotas, and to keep the "Postmaster" and "Root" aliases read by someone.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing to one person should read like a polite conversation. Keep it short, do not shout, assume anyone can read it, and wait until you have cooled down before sending an angry reply.

sections.title: One-to-Many Communication: Lists and NetNews
sections.content:
Everything that applies to mail applies when writing to many people, with the added risk of offending a great many more of them, so knowing the audience matters. The general advice for mailing lists and newsgroups is to read both for one to two months before posting anything, to understand the culture of the group. Consider that a large audience will see the posting, possibly including your present or next boss, and that lists and newsgroups are frequently archived, so words may be stored for a long time in a place many people can reach. Messages should be brief and to the point, and subject lines should follow the conventions of the group.

Replying needs care. A reply often goes back to the address that originated the post, which is often the address of the whole list or group, so it is best to type the address rather than rely on "reply". Summarize the original at the top of the reply, because a reader may meet the reply before the original. Do not use delivery receipts, non-delivery notices or vacation programs on lists; they are unreliable across systems, invasive, and some people see them as an invasion of privacy. Do not get involved in flame wars. If a personal message goes to a list, apologize to the person and to the group, and argue with one person by mail rather than on the list.

For mailing lists specifically, send subscribe and unsubscribe messages to the right address, often a "-request" alias, save the subscription messages because they usually explain how to unsubscribe, and remember that a sent message cannot be retrieved. Do not send large files when a URL or an ftp pointer will do. If you ask a question, post a summary of the answers. Some lists are private, and mail from them must not be reported to a wider audience.

NetNews, the globally distributed system of topical groups, is divided into hierarchies such as sci for science, comp for computers, news for discussion of NetNews itself, rec for recreation, soc for social issues, talk for long discussions, biz for business, and alt, whose groups are created outside the usual process. Read a whole thread before replying, avoid "Me Too" posts, and make sure a follow-up post says more than the text it quotes. Cross-post to a few related groups rather than posting separately to each, warn readers if you use Followup-To, and cancel only your own articles. Posts that spoil a movie or book are marked "Spoilers" in the Subject line. Off-topic advertising is treated as nothing less than criminal, and forging news articles is censured, although software such as PGP can produce a fingerprint that detects manipulation.
sections.plainLanguage: Posting to a group means writing for many readers at once, some of whom you will never meet. Read the group first, keep to the topic, and check the reply address before you press send.

sections.title: Administrator and Moderator Guidelines
sections.content:
Administrators of lists and news servers have their own duties. The memo asks them to clarify their site's policies on subscribing to and posting to groups and mailing lists, including any disclaimers in signatures, and to publicize their archive policy, including how long articles are kept. They should consider how long to keep system logs and publicize that policy too, investigate accusations about their users promptly and with an open mind, and monitor the health of the system.

For mailing lists, keep them up to date to avoid the "bouncing mail" problem, help list owners when problems arise, and inform them of maintenance windows or planned downtime. Keep "-request" aliases for subscription and administration, and make sure all mail gateways operate smoothly. For NetNews, publicize the nature of the feed the site receives, since users may want to know why it is not a full feed. Be aware that the multiplicity of news reader clients may cause the news server to be blamed for problems in the clients. Honour requests to cancel a user's own posts or invalid posts, such as chain letters, immediately. Have "Usenet", "Netnews" and "News" aliased, and make sure someone reads that mail.

Moderators have their own list. Post the Frequently Asked Questions at regular intervals, including the guidelines for articles and messages, and if you are not the FAQ maintainer, make sure someone does. Maintain a welcome message that contains subscribe and unsubscribe information, and post the group's charter or guidelines regularly. Keep mailing lists and newsgroups up to date, post messages in a timely fashion, and designate a substitute when you go on vacation or out of town.
sections.plainLanguage: The people who run a list or a news server carry most of the burden of keeping it orderly. The memo asks them to publish their rules, keep the lists current, and be there when a user needs help.

sections.title: Information Services
sections.content:
The third part covers the information services that were growing quickly: Gopher, Wais, the World Wide Web, ftp, telnet, and the real-time services MUDs, MOOs and IRC. The basic point for users is that all of these belong to someone else, and the people who pay the bills make the rules; information may be free or it may not. Check local configuration, software setup and network connections before assuming a problem is the provider's fault. Do not assume that any information you find is up to date or accurate, since new technologies allow almost anyone to be a publisher, but not everyone has discovered the responsibilities that come with publishing.

Unless you are sure that security and authentication technology is in use, anything you submit travels over the Internet in the clear, with no protection from "sniffers" or forgers. Use a nearby mirror server when one is listed for a popular server. Do not deposit files on someone else's ftp site, which the memo calls dumping and says is not generally acceptable. Spread the system load on popular sites by avoiding rush hour and logging in during off-peak times. In real-time services, listen first to learn the culture of the group, do not greet everyone in a channel personally or use a client's automation to do it, respect a user's nickname, and do not badger other users for personal information such as age or location.

Administrators are told to make clear what may be copied and what may not, to describe what the site and organization offer, and to keep general policies clear. Keep information, especially READMEs, up to date and provide them in plain ascii text. Present a list of mirrors with the copyright that applies to them and their update schedule. Use conventional file extensions, and make file names unique in their first eight characters. Make sure the site has something unique to offer rather than pointing at other services, and do not point to other sites without asking first. Test applications with a variety of clients instead of assuming everything works because one client works, and assume the low end of technology for clients. Date time-sensitive materials, understand export restrictions before posting, and tell users what you plan to do with any information you collect, such as web feedback, including a warning if their statements will be published.
sections.plainLanguage: Services like Gopher, the Web and ftp belong to somebody else, and the people paying for them set the rules. Use them carefully, keep your own copies current, and tell people what you do with anything they send you.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Status
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in this memo. The security guidance appears inside the guidelines themselves: assume mail is not secure unless you use encryption, treat anything submitted to an information service as travelling in the clear, and expect forgery and spoofing in mail and news of varying degrees of detectability.

The status statement says the memo provides information for the Internet community and does not specify an Internet standard of any kind. Its distribution is unlimited. A selected bibliography of books, frequently asked questions and guides follows the guidelines, and the memo notes that items not found in those works were gathered from the experience of the IETF RUN Working Group.
sections.plainLanguage: This is advice, not a standard, and it does not cover computer security in depth. Its security advice is scattered through the guidelines themselves.

items.title: Signature
items.text: No longer than 4 lines, so readers can tell who sent the message.

items.title: File size
items.text: Do not send a file larger than 50 Kilobytes; use file transfer or smaller pieces.

items.title: Capital letters
items.text: Use mixed case; upper case looks as if you are shouting.

items.title: Subject line
items.text: Make it describe the content of the message.

items.title: Reply address
items.text: Type the address instead of relying on reply, so a private message does not reach the whole list.
